partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a 2-bedroom ground floor maisonette with their adult children. Several members of the household have long-term physical health conditions. The resident first reported damp and mould concerns to their housing officer on 26 January 2024. The resident first reported boiler faults on 15 January 2024. The resident raised their complaint on 28 February 2024 about damp and mould present in the property and faults with the boiler. A new boiler was installed at the property on 6 March 2024. The resident contacted the landlord again on 13 March 2024 explaining they were experiencing issues with the heating and that 3 radiators were not heating up properly. Work was carried out to the boiler and a mould wash was completed in the bedroom and living room between 18 March and 18 April 2024 over 4 visits. The resident asked to escalate their complaint to stage 2 on 7 April 2024 because repairs had not been completed and they wanted compensation. The landlord offered £94 compensation for boiler replacement delays in its stage 2 response on 7 May 2024.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not appropriately investigate the cause of the damp and mould when the resident first reported these concerns. This delayed the completion of the works needed to resolve the issue.
The landlord's communication with the resident was also poor.

The landlord did not respond to the resident's concerns about the boiler within its published timescales and left them without a working boiler for around a week. It provided an apology and appropriate compensation for the delay.
The complaint was responded to in line with the landlord's complaints policy.

partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a 2-bedroom ground floor maisonette with adult children, and several household members have long-term physical health conditions. The complaint concerned the landlord’s response to reports of damp and mould, faults with the boiler, and complaint handling. On 28 February 2024 the resident complained about damp and mould at the property and faults with the boiler. A new boiler was installed on 6 March 2024. On 13 March 2024 the resident contacted the landlord again about heating issues and 3 radiators not heating properly. On 14 March 2024 the landlord issued its stage 1 response, saying work was booked for radiators and for damp and mould, and it did not identify failings or offer compensation. Between 18 March and 18 April 2024 work was carried out to the boiler and a mould wash was completed in the bedroom and living room over 4 visits. On 7 April 2024 the resident asked to escalate the complaint to stage 2 because repairs had not been completed and they wanted compensation. On 7 May 2024 the landlord issued its stage 2 response, identified that compensation should have been offered at stage 1 for delays to the boiler replacement, offered £94 compensation for those delays, and said some damp and mould work was ongoing. The resident asked the Ombudsman to investigate because they were unhappy with repair delays and did not accept the landlord’s offer of redress.

orders: Landlord must apologise in writing to the resident for the failures identified.
Landlord must pay the resident £400 for failures in handling reports of damp and mould.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not appropriately investigate the cause of the damp and mould when the resident first reported these concerns. This delayed the completion of the works needed to resolve the issue.
The repairs needed here took significantly longer than this. This was a failing.

The impact of this delay on the resident was significant. They had expressed concerns over the impact of the damp and mould on them and their family, and the landlord did not show that this concern was taken seriously.
Because of the extent of the delay and impact, we find there was maladministration in the landlord’s response to the resident’s reports of damp and mould.
The landlord apologised for the delays and provided compensation in line with its policy at stage 2 of the complaints process.
As the landlord responded to the resident’s complaint within its policy timescales at both stages, we find there was no maladministration in its complaint handling.
